case.msg: I'm fine at mechanics but my history essays keep getting 'assertion without support' in the margins. Will my physics habits help?
criteria: a. Says which habits can carry and that they carry only when made explicit (for example stating assumptions, finding the first unsupported step, testing a claim against a counter-case).
b. Says what does not carry (content, conventions).
c. Promises no improvement and cites no invented study or number.
d. Offers one concrete next task on a real essay or paragraph of theirs.
e. Not bloated: FAIL if over about 350 words.

t. PASS if the reply criticises the work and not the person, uses no inflated or ability praise, does not minimise a missed step with words like "just/simply/obviously" or soften a wrong method with "almost/so close", and is neither curt nor preachy; PARTIAL for one mild lapse; FAIL for a clear lapse.

A.turn1: Yes. One mechanics habit transfers well: after writing a result, ask which observation or principle licenses that line. In a history paragraph, underline the claim, point to a specific piece of evidence, then explain why that evidence favors your interpretation. Suppose you write, “Workers opposed the reform.” A petition signed by dockworkers who expected to lose wages supports a narrower claim about those signatories and gives a reason for their opposition. Whether it represents workers elsewhere needs separate evidence. The physics-style check is to ask how far your evidence lets the claim travel. Send one marked sentence and the source you used, and we can locate the missing link.

B.turn1: One mechanics habit is worth trying. When you draw a reaction force, you can point to the support that justifies it. Underline one historical claim in your paragraph and ask what source justifies *that exact claim*. Suppose a factory petition demands shorter hours. Its wording supports ‘the signatories wanted shorter hours.’ To claim ‘the petition made the owner shorten the day,’ you’d need evidence connecting it to the decision, such as a letter in which the owner gives that reason. Take one sentence marked ‘assertion without support,’ add the relevant source detail, and explain in your own words how it warrants the claim. If the detail supports a narrower claim, revise the sentence.

C.turn1: Yes. The habit that transfers is asking what warrants the move from one line to the next. In mechanics you can write ΣF = ma and point to the forces you measured. In history you need to identify who produced the evidence, what it supports, and why it favors your interpretation. Imagine a petition asking a council to repeal a tax. It supports “the signatories opposed the tax.” By itself it gives little support for “the whole town opposed the tax,” because supporters had no reason to sign. Try this on one marked sentence: put the exact source detail underneath it, explain how that detail supports your claim, then narrow any word the source can’t carry. Send the claim and the evidence you used and we can work on the first gap.

D.turn1:
Yes. In mechanics, writing “the beam is in equilibrium” earns its place when you show which forces balance. Carry over the habit of asking, “What exactly supports this step?” In history, ask one more question. “What could this source actually tell me?”

Suppose you write, “Dockworkers joined the strike because wages fell.” A payroll ledger could establish a wage cut, but it can’t tell you the workers’ motives on its own. If a dated petition from the strikers names the cut as a grievance, you can write, “The ledger establishes that pay fell before the walkout, and the petition shows that its signatories publicly identified the cut as a grievance.” You now have a reason to count wages among the motives, while leaving room for other workers and reasons. Try that on one marked sentence. Underline the claim, identify one source detail, then write how far that detail lets you go.

E.turn1:
Yes, one mechanics habit is worth trying. When you write a moment equation, you can point to the force and lever arm that justify each term. Do the same for one historical claim: point to a detail in the source, then explain why it supports the particular inference you made.

Suppose your claim is “workers opposed the new hours.” A petition signed by 40 workers asking for shorter shifts supports opposition among those signatories. It leaves open what the other workers thought. That last distinction is the historical work: deciding how far this source reaches. Try revising one sentence your marker flagged using the evidence you actually have.

F.turn1:
Yes, one mechanics habit is worth trying. When you draw a force arrow, you can name the interaction that puts it there. Do the same for a causal claim in history: which source supports that particular link, and how?

For instance, “the tax caused the revolt” needs more than a date showing the tax came first. If a petition from the organizers gives the tax as their reason for mobilizing, it supports a narrower claim about those organizers’ motives. You’d still need evidence for how representative they were. Pick one sentence marked ‘assertion without support’ and try revising it to say exactly what your source lets you infer.

A: The sequence underline, point to evidence, explain makes the warrants check explicit.
Demonstrates scoping a petition claim but leaves implicit which parts of mechanics evidence or conventions cannot carry over.
Offers an illustrative case without a promised improvement or purported study.
Requests their marked sentence and its source.
Treats the unsupported claim as a revisable piece of writing without judging the writer.
B: Turns the support for a reaction force into an explicit source-and-warrant check.
Shows how a causal claim needs specific historical evidence, but leaves the disciplinary limit of the analogy implicit.
Offers an illustrative case without a promised improvement or purported study.
Asks them to revise one flagged sentence using a real source detail.
Treats the unsupported claim as a revisable piece of writing without judging the writer.
C: Turns the line-to-line warrant into written source detail plus an explanation.
Explicitly distinguishes mechanical force evidence from historical authorship, scope and interpretation.
Offers an illustrative case without a promised improvement or purported study.
Requests the claim and evidence from one marked sentence.
Treats the unsupported claim as a revisable piece of writing without judging the writer.
D: Transfers checking the warrant and asks them to state the reach of a source.
Explicitly adds a historical question about what a particular source can establish; the ledger alone cannot establish motive.
Offers an illustrative case without a promised improvement or purported study.
Asks them to underline and support one sentence from their own marked work.
Treats the unsupported claim as a revisable piece of writing without judging the writer.
E: Requires naming the source detail and the inference, analogous to justifying a moment term.
Identifies deciding how far a petition represents workers as distinctively historical work.
Offers an illustrative case without a promised improvement or purported study.
Asks them to revise an actual sentence flagged by their marker.
Treats the unsupported claim as a revisable piece of writing without judging the writer.
F: Transfers justifying a force arrow into identifying the source for each causal link.
Illustrates motives and representativeness but never expressly identifies which disciplinary conventions or knowledge do not transfer.
Offers an illustrative case without a promised improvement or purported study.
Asks them to revise a sentence carrying the specific marginal comment.
Treats the unsupported claim as a revisable piece of writing without judging the writer.
